sceneHappening: Lawsuits among believers, a warning about wrongdoing, and the body as the Lord's temple
summary: Paul is shocked that a believer with a grievance against another would go to court before unbelievers instead of the saints. The saints will judge the world and angels, so surely they can judge small matters. Better to be wronged or defrauded than to go to law against a brother, and in fact they are the ones doing wrong. Then a warning: "Don't you know that the unrighteous will not inherit God's Kingdom?" He lists wrongdoers, including the sexually immoral, idolaters, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, slanderers, and swindlers, and says, "Such were some of you. But you were washed. But you were sanctified. But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God." Next he takes up a slogan, "All things are lawful for me," and answers that not all things are helpful, and that he will not be mastered by anything. Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, but the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. God raised the Lord and will raise us up. Their bodies are members of Christ, and joining oneself to a prostitute makes one body with her. "Flee sexual immorality." The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and "you are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body."
whySettingMatters: In the Roman world, lawsuits were a tool of the powerful: wealthy citizens could take poorer ones to court, and judges often favored people of status. Paul's concern is partly that Christians are using the courts to attack each other, in front of outsiders, over what he calls trivial matters. The "all things are lawful for me" in 6:12 is probably a Corinthian slogan, which Paul quotes and corrects, and so is probably "food is for the stomach" (6:13). The vice list in 6:9-10 includes two words, malakoi and arsenokoitai, whose exact meaning is debated among translators and scholars; translations vary, and readers should consult commentaries rather than lean on a single English word. Prostitution was common in a port city, and some Corinthians may have thought what the body did did not matter for the spirit; Paul answers that the body belongs to the Lord and will be raised. "Bought with a price" uses a slave-market word, which would be heard in a city full of slaves and freed people.

people.note: Appalled at lawsuits and at casual sexual immorality.
Told they will judge the world and belong to Christ.
Lord of the body; the One whose name washes, sanctifies, and justifies.

questions: Paul says it is better to be wronged than to take a fellow believer to court. When is that hard, and when might it not apply?
"Such were some of you." How does that sentence hold both honesty about sin and hope?
Paul quotes a slogan, "all things are lawful," and then corrects it. Which slogans do we use that need the same correction?
"You are not your own." What does it mean to say the body belongs to the Lord?
